This is omitted from the present Bill, and I think it would be a great mistake to eliminate it from this legislation, because it is telling a company which enjoys all the privileges that many gas companies enjoy, that they shall supply the consumer with a sufficient supply of gas, especially in the cold season of the year when gas is very much required. I do not think the minister should ask us to eliminate such an important section when it means so much to the people of Ontario who are being supplied with natural gas at the present time.

maintopic: INSPECTION OF GAS AND GAS METERS
speechtext: I am informed that that has been left out of the present Bill because the opinion has been given that we have not the power to enforce it. We might, however, go through with the remaining clauses of the Bill, and then I will leave the Bill in committee and we can take it up again and consider it a little further.

maintopic: INSPECTION OF GAS AND GAS METERS
speechtext: Clause 19 is not closed so far as the committee is concerned?

maintopic: INSPECTION OF GAS AND GAS METERS
speechtext:
It was not
clause 19 that was particularly referred to. Another point was raised there which my hon. friend (Mr. McCoig) contended was of vital importance, that it was in the old Act and that it was not brought into this. I suggested that, as we had an opinion from the Minister of Justice that we had not powers with reference to that, we could not do that under our powers, that we might pass these other sections, and I would allow the Bill to remain in committee until I had an opportunity of consulting the Minister of Justice with reference to the matter. Then it could he brought up again. I will not ask that the Bill be passed until I have an opportunity of doing that.

maintopic: INSPECTION OF GAS AND GAS METERS
speechtext: The Bill will be brought up in committee again.

maintopic: INSPECTION OF GAS AND GAS METERS
speechtext: Yes.

Section agreed to.
On section 20-for offence specific penalty for which is not provided:

maintopic: INSPECTION OF GAS AND GAS METERS
speechtext: How does this read with the amendment passed a few minutes ago reducing the minimum penalty to $5?

maintopic: INSPECTION OF GAS AND GAS METERS
speechtext:
This would be a blanket for all the rest. That was a
special penalty for a special case. This will provide for other cases which are not provided for specially.

Section agreed to.
Progress reported.

maintopic: EXCHEQUER COURT ACT AMENDMENT

speechtext: Right Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) moved the second reading of Bill No. 19, to amend the Exchequer Court Act.

maintopic: EXCHEQUER COURT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I do not know that copies of this Bill have been distributed as yet.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: EXCHEQUER COURT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: They have been distributed, I understand.

maintopic: EXCHEQUER COURT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I would
point out to my right hon. friend that this Bill does not appear to be on the official fyle. Copies of the Bill may be lying on the table, but I do not think hon. members have had an opportunity of perusing the provisions of the Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: EXCHEQUER COURT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Of course, I have no
desire to proceed with the Bill if any hon. gentleman thinks he has not had proper opportunity of perusing it, but as I explained the other day, it is a very simple Bill, very easy of apprehension, and I would not anticipate there would be serious objection to it. There are two clauses. Their purpose is to provide that on appeals from the decisions of the Commissioner of Patents, which appeals under the existing law lie to the Exchequer Court, and are brought at the instance of the party interested, the Commissioner of Patents, as representing the Crown and the public interest, shall as matter of right be entitled to be heard before the Exchequer Court, and shall, in the event of the decision of the Exchequer Court reversing the decision of the Commissioner have the right of appeal to the Supreme Court. I may say that until 1913 the only appeal from the decision of the Commissioner of Patents was to the Governor General in Council. At the time that was not considered a suitable means of rectifying any error that the Commissioner might fall into, and in consequence, by an Act passed in that year, the appeal was made to the Exchequer Court instead of to the Governor in Council. That appeal, of course,

was at the instance of the party interested. Though there was no provision in that law for the Commissioner of Patents being represented before the Exchequer Court, as a matter of practice he always has been so represented. My information is that the judge of the Exchequer Court thought it desirable tlhat the other side of the case should be put, and at his suggestion the Commissioner of Patents appeared and defended his view.
That practice has gone on without question until a recent case. In that recent case the decision of the Exchequer Court was favourable to the private party and adverse to the decision of the Commissioner of Patents. The latter, assuming, apparently, from the well-established practice, that he was a proper party in the case made an application for leave to appeal to one of the judges of the Supreme Court. That application was necessary because upon the question arising there was no amount involved, and therefore no sum of $500. The commissioner made his application to the judge for leave to appeal, and the judge presiding declined to grant leave to appeal, taking the position that the Commissioner of Patents was not a party to the case and, therefore, in effect had no standing even before the Exchequer Court, and, of course, no right of appeal to the Supreme Court. Now the purpose of this Bill is simply to convert into a legal right what by practice was recognized as the privilege of the commissioner, to appear before the Exchequer Court to defend his decision. Of course, it was not at all in the interests of the commissioner himself that that right should be recognized, but it was felt that there should be somebody to represent the public interest, to put before the court that public interest and the reasons why in that public interest the decision of the commissioner should be maintained. This present Bill provides simply for that right to the commissioner to appear before the Exchequer Court and uphold the public interest in the matter, and, in the event of the Exchequer Court deciding adversely, to carry the case to appeal, just as the private party has the right to carry the case to appeal. The object, in a word, is to put the public on a footing of equality with the private interest, and I would think there would be general consent that there should be such a provision.

maintopic: EXCHEQUER COURT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I do not find any
fault with the purpose of this Bill, to give the commissioner the right of appeal

which the private party enjoys, but what I would suggest is this: here is a matter that refers exclusively to the Patent Act, just as Chapter 17 of the Statutes of 1913 which transferred all appeals from the Governor in Council, and even all pending cases, if I remember rightly, to the Exchequer Court, refers exclusively to the Patent Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: EXCHEQUER COURT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: The object of this Bill is to amend the Exchequer Court Act.

maintopic: EXCHEQUER COURT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I know, and that is where confusion may arise. The fact of amending the Exchequer Court Act in order to give a certain person mentioned only in the Patent Act, and whose duties are defined by the Patent Act, the right of appeal might embarrass anyone looking up the legislation on the matter. There are always in the Patent Act certain provisions whereby an appeal lies from the decision of the commissioner. Now, why not include the provisions of the present Bill in the Patent Act, so that anyone looking up the legislation would not have to turn up the Exchequer Court Act to find out whether the commissioner had the right of appeal? If we are to give the commissioner the right of appeal by amending the Exchequer Court Act, one could not tell by looking up the Patent Act that he had that right Under the consolidation he would find that the appeal lies with the Exchequer Court, but he would have to look under the head of "Exchequer Court" to find a matter which is exclusively and entirely within the purview of the Patent Act. The Bill is all right. I do not want my hon. friend to think that I am criticising its principle; my only objection is in regard to the place which the title occupies in the statute. My object is to make the work easier for lawyers looking up the Patent Act to ascertain what the powers and the rights of appeal are, instead of having to look up the Exchequer Court Act.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: EXCHEQUER COURT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I rather fear the House is getting into matters of detail which can properly be discussed only in committee. The hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) states that he has no fault to find with the principle of the Bill, with which he is satisfied. The only question involved in his objection is one which it would be well to discuss in committee.

maintopic: EXCHEQUER COURT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I submit, Mr. Speaker, that changing the title of the Bill would be changing the whole Bill.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: EXCHEQUER COURT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
That does not involve the principle of the Bill.

Motion agreed to and bill read the second time, and on motion of Hon. Mr. Doherty the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Boivin in the chair.
On Section 1-Commissioner of Patents may appear by Counsel.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: EXCHEQUER COURT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I quite realize there is a good deal of force, from the point of view of convenience, in that suggestion that the hon. member for Three Rivers fnakes. But unfortunately the practice has been to cover the entire jurisdiction of the Exchequer Court by the provisions in the Exchequer Court Act, and this particular provision does not differ from others, if I am correctly informed. You look to the Exchequer Court Act, for the jurisdiction of the Exchequer Court, and there you find also a great variety of matters referred to. But it is there you go to ascertain the jurisdiction of that Court. The suggestion of the hon. gentleman, if it were to be useful, would involve the repealing of the Act of 1913 to which I think people have become thoroughly accustomed, and re-enacting it as an amendment to the Patent Act. While that might perhaps be advisable from the point of view of convenience, and while it might be well to put a clause into the Patent Act to say that there is an appeal to the Exchequer Court, I still think that the Exchequer Court Act is the proper place to regulate the jurisdiction of that Court, as likewise the right of appeal from the Exchequer Court to the Supreme Court. We might consider the desirability of putting a clause into the Pat-tent Act, if it is not there, to indicate that there is an appeal to the Exchequer Court, but in the meantime it would be well to let this bill pass. We are not here conferring jurisdiction on the Exchequer Court; that is already conferred by the existing Act. We are only making provision as to who shall be entitled to be heard before the Exchequer Court, and providing a right of appeal for both parties.	As the law stands at
present, the Exchequer Court has jurisdiction, and the appeal exists. The only difficulty is that it is now interpreted to mean that only one party can be heard before the Exchequer Court and only one party can appeal. We are not creating the appeal; we are simply providing that both parties may be heard on an appeal which already is provided for in the Exchequer Court Act.

maintopic: EXCHEQUER COURT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: The statement of the minister gives more force to my suggestion. We are not conferring jurisdiction on the Exchequer Court; it already has jurisdiction. The only question is that an officer who comes within the scope of a specific Act, namely, the Commissioner of Patents, shall have the right to appeal to that court. The gist of the thing is not the right of appeal or the question of jurisdiction, tjut the right of the commissioner; and if you were looking for his powers, if you wanted to find out whether he had a right of appeal, you would naturally look to the Patent Act under the duties and powers of the commissioner. I do not object to this Bill being passed, but it creates confusion. My hon. friend knows better than any one else that if you have to go through five or six statutes having reference to different matters in order to find out what particular officer has to do, you are put to considerable labour and sometimes confusion is created. My object is to put under one heading and in one Act all the powers and privileges conferred upon this particular officer.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: EXCHEQUER COURT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
This Bill does not
create the appeal. It does not give the right of appeal even to the Commissioner of Patents. It only provides that on an appeal from the decision of the Commissioner of Patents, which appeal can only be by the other parties and which already exists and is provided for in the Exchequer Court Act, the Commissioner of Patents shall be entitled to be heard. Then having once given him that right to be heard, we give him the same right to appeal from that decision that already exists in favour of the other party. So that we are in reality only regulating the procedure. There is convenience in confining the entire jurisdiction and procedure before the Exchequer Court in the Exchequer Court Act, and this is a matter of procedure. Before the section passes I desire to amend it to some extent. I do not know that it is necessary, but perhaps it is as well to put in the amendment which I shall propose. It has reference to the way in which the Commissioner of Patents is entitled to appeal. I would also move to insert, after the word "patents" in the eleventh line, the words "acting in the said capacity."

maintopic: EXCHEQUER COURT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, the right hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) means, by the terms of his amendment, that the Commissioner of Patents shall have the right to appear for the Crown and as representing the inter-



ests of the public. If he adds " representing the interests of the public," and should the Supreme Court find against the opinion of the commissioner, should we infer that the finding is contrary to the interests of the public?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: EXCHEQUER COURT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: (Translation.) There are two interests to be represented: on the one side the interest of the party applying for the patent; then, against that, is the interest of the public, which may require that the patent be withheld; and there is the interest of the Crown. The commissioner will represent the public at large interested in its with-holdment. It may not be absolutely necessary to say that he has the right to appear as representing the. Crown and also as representing the interests of the public, but I do not see what objection there could be to it. There are cases where the Crown may appear by reason of having a special interest in the matter. There are others, as in the present case, in which the Crown is interested in appearing not in order to protect a special interest of the Crown, but in the interests of the public at large. Such seems to be the case on hand.

maintopic: EXCHEQUER COURT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: (Translation.) I understand the explanation given by the right hon. Minister of Justice, but I believe that we may take as a principle in law that in a case where the Government is represented, the Government, through its representative, appears for the Crown. Now, under our constitution, the Crown represents the public in a general way, and if in a clause of our law we say that any one represents the Crown, I take it that we infer thereby that this person appears for the public in a general way. By adding that this person appears not only for the Crown but also in the interest of the public, we either make a distinction which should not be found in our laws, or it constitutes a tautology, which is not necessary. I believe that by saying, "The Commissioner of Patents, in the name of the Crown, shall have the right to appear . . ." the phraseology would be better and the idea more constitutional.

speakeroldname: The Right Hon. C. J. DOHERTY:
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: EXCHEQUER COURT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: (Translation.) I should congratulate myself over the fact that the hon. member so completely admits that, the Government represents the interests of the whole public-

maintopic: EXCHEQUER COURT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: (Translation.) As a legal fiction.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: EXCHEQUER COURT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: (Translation.) But I might perhaps acknowledge the tautology, for I confess that the phrase is not absolutely necessary. However, notwithstanding the respect I have for the opinion of the hon. member, I conceive that there are cases where the Crown, that is to say, the Government, acts as being itself interested, that is to say, by reason of the organized government as such having an interest therein; and there are other cases-such as this one-where the Government as such [DOT] is in no way interested in a patent being granted or denied to the applicant. In this case the interested party is the public in general. Though I admit that there would be no necessity of saying so expressly, it appears nevertheless desirable to indicate clearly in what capacity our commissioners are to be recognized and it can do no harm to state that they not only represent the Crown but have the special object of protecting an interest which is not so much that of the Crown as of the public in general. I concede that the Crown has the right to protect the interests of the public in general but if one refers simply to the general law, it is the Attorney General who should intervene to represent these interests. I wish to make it clear that the commissioner can, as representative of the public interests, lodge this appeal, as well as the Attorney General.

maintopic: EXCHEQUER COURT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, I am astonished to hear the hon. Minister of Justice advance this argument. We are in a British country. We live under British institutions, and in framing our legislation, we should, as far as possible, follow the principle of the British Constitution. I do not believe that in our public law, any more than in our private legislation, there could be a distinction between the Crown, as representative of the executive power of the judicial power, and of the people. It is very different in the United States. In that country I understand that one can say "The people vs. so and so," "The State vs. so and so;" but in a British country there can be no question of the people against an individual or of the State against an individual it is always the Crown. I am even more astonished to hear the right hon. Minister of Justice suggest a case where the interests of the Crown, in the acceptatioon of the word I have just indicated, might conflict with the interests of the people in a general way. How could it happen in a case before the Supreme Court that there might be con-

flict between the interest of the Government-the word Government, according to what the hon. Minister of Justice has just said, would then mean the Crown-and the interest of the general public? Who then would represent the general public? Who would have a mandate to represent the general public, according to the principles of our Constitution? Who could present himself before the Supreme Court-not only before the Supreme Court but before any court of our country-and say, " 1 represent the interests of the general public?" And how again could the commissioner or his representative claim to have the mandate to represent before the Supreme Court the interests of the general public, if these conflicted with those of the Crown? Who would represent the Crown? Could the Commissioner of Patents, as an officer of the Government, as one of the Crown's representatives, claim that he represented the interests of the general public as opposed to those of the Crown? I believe that as a legal proposition, it would hardily be defensible. Certainly my experience is much more limited than that of the minister, but I cannot conceive of cases where the Government could be represented by a lawyer who would go before the Supreme Court and claim that he represented the interests of the general public and that these interests were opposed to those of the Crown. A lawyer who would appear and uphold interests opposed to those of the Crown could not be the representative of the Government according to the principles which govern our Coustitution.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: EXCHEQUER COURT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, we might no doubt prolong this very interesting discussion in dwelling upon the part taken in it by the hon. member for Dorchester, but it would not lead to very important practical results. I will only say that I was misunderstood if it was believed that I had suggested that there could be interests of the Crown opposed to those of the general public. My proposition was, that, among the interests that the Crown is called upon to defend and protect, one might make a distinction between those of the Crown proper, so called, and those of the public, which the Crown, as its representative, is charged with protecting. Now these two interests usually are protected through the intermediary of the Attorney General. In this case under consideration, we make an exception as to the official who would appear to protect these interests, and we
designate this official to represent the interests that are as a rule represented by the Attorney General. It seems to me that in any case there is no harm in stating it. I admit the thing would go without saying, and as is often repeated-the remark was first made by a great man-things that go without saying are still better when said.

maintopic: EXCHEQUER COURT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
(Translation.) Would
the object of the amendment then be that of removing all responsibility from the commissioner showing that he is acting as a representative of the Crown?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: EXCHEQUER COURT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: (Translation.) Yes.

maintopic: EXCHEQUER COURT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: (Translation.) In that case, why not insert the phrase "es-qualite"? It is short, it is understood by every one, and it would show exactly in what capacity he comes before the Court.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: EXCHEQUER COURT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: (Translation.) These words would be better understood in our province than in any other part of the country. I do not know that these words have the same meaning in the English provinces as they have in our laws. Besides, even in saying "es-qualite," we do not specify in what capacity. There are several capacities. We say "es-qualite" when one appears as a tutor or as a curator. Could it be wrong to embody in the law not only that he appears es-qualite, but also state in which capacity?

maintopic: EXCHEQUER COURT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: (Translation.) Would not the English words "Acting in his official capacity" translate the words "es-qualite"?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: EXCHEQUER COURT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: (Translation.) I do not think they would, not in the present instance; because if we say "In his official capacity," this would not mean In the capacity of Commissioner of Patents. We are simply granting him a new power. I do not know that I would have moved this amendment had I known that it would be objected to.

maintopic: EXCHEQUER COURT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: (Translation.) I am not objecting, I am merely asking for information.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: EXCHEQUER COURT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: (Translation.) I believe the best reason is that one which I gave in reply to the hon. member for Dorchester. I do not think it wrong to say things sometimes which are not absolutely necessary.

maintopic: EXCHEQUER COURT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
(Translation.) Mr. Chairman, the clause such as it reads before the hon. minister moved the amend-

ment was the following: "The Commissioner of Patents has the right to appear and be heard through his lawyer, on the hearing of the appeal." The hon. minister now sug-gests/ that we add: "The Commissioner of Patents, on behalf of the Crown and as representing the interests of the public, shall have the right to appear and be heard through his lawyer, on the hearing of the appeal." Who shall decide if the commissioner appears for the Crown or if he does so in the interests of the public?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: EXCHEQUER COURT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: (Translation.) There shall be no necessity of a decision, for he shall have to do both. The amendment reads "On behalf of the Crown and as representing the interests of the public." If there are two distinct interests, he must represent both.

maintopic: EXCHEQUER COURT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
(Translation.) As I
said, before, there can be no distinction from the legal and the constitutional point -of view, between the interests of the Crown and the interests of the public. Therefore, as the hon. minister has just said, if there is no distinction, there is no reason to add "the interests of the public" after saying "on behalf of the Crown" this being sufficient. The right hon. minister told us just a while ago, that there were cases *where a distinction might exist. Now, he tells us that such a distinction does not exist. If it does not exist, then if amounts to what I said: It is a case of redundancy, and it would be better to eliminate the last part of the amendment, in due regard for the principles of the constitution as well as for the improvement of our legal phraseology.

maintopic: EXCHEQUER COURT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
(Translation.) Will the right 'hon. minister allow me to remark that there is a clause, in the patents law, which might properly apply to the case mentioned by the hon. member for Dorchester, namely, when an employee in the civil service asks for a patent. This employee has no right to obtain it for himself, unless he ask the government; there is a provision to the effect that the government is to be served first. The commissioner is the one who shall decide on what terms the patent may be granted. In a case like this, the interests of the public may differ from those of the Crown; and then, the commissioner cannot represent both interests at the same time, because in his official capacity, he will have to repre- * sent the Crown and refuse to grant the patent to the employee, or else make such

terms as would not be in the interests of the public generally. The words "or" instead of "and" should therefore be inserted, so that when a conflict should arise, he could choose between the two.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: EXCHEQUER COURT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
(Translation.) How then conciliate the opinion of my hon. friend from Dorchester witlj that of my hon. friend from Three Rivers? I am indeed on the horns of a dilemma.
It is obvious that I could not please both the hon. members at the same time, because my hon. friend from Three Rivers gives us to understand that in some cases the fact that the commissioner would be serving the interest of the Crown would preclude the idea that he was acting in the interest of the whole people.

maintopic: EXCHEQUER COURT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
(Translation.)	Not
necessarily.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: EXCHEQUER COURT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
(Translation.) No, but I think the hon. member from Three Rivers came to my rescue during the discussion in which I was engaged with my hon. friend from Dorchester.
The hon. gentleman is supposing a case in which the commissioner, when claiming on behalf of the Crown a royalty from the man who is trying to use his patent, would be there to uphold the rights of the Crown as to the collection of a certain sum. Now, I do not deny that the people are indirectly concerned in that matter. All that is added to the public revenue benefits the people. However, such is not the case when it is a matter of safeguarding a right which each individual is directly entitled to. In fact, when it is a question whether a man is entitled to a patent or not, if he obtains it to whose detriment is it? To the detriment of the public who, by the fact this patent is granted, is debarred from using such an article. True, it is in a sense that the public is interested, even when the question is what amount should a man pay as a royalty for the privilege of availing himself of a patent. As I said a few minutes ago, although the Crown is primarily interested as collector of the revenue the people who are benefited by it are also interested.

maintopic: EXCHEQUER COURT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
(Translation.) The
commissioner has the right to prevent the use of that patent, and it might be in the public interest that such a patent should be used.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: EXCHEQUER COURT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: (Translation.) In that sense, yes.

maintopic: PENSION DEDUCTIONS FOR RETURNED SOLDIERS INSURANCE

speakeroldname: Mr. C. G. POWER (Quebec South) moved:
maintopic: PENSION DEDUCTIONS FOR RETURNED SOLDIERS INSURANCE
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, it is expedient, in order that a greater number of disabled soldiers and dependents be enabled to enjoy the benefits of the Returned Soldiers' Insurance Act, that arrangements be made to, at the request of the Pensioner, deduct from Pension payments such sums as the said Pensioner shall indicate and apply same to the payment of insurance premiums under the said Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the resolution is a very simple one. Under authority of an Act passed last session, the Government has entered into a plan of insurance for returned soldiers and their dependents. Although the Returned Soldiers' Insurance Act has not been in force very long, it seems to have been productive of good results. I am informed that a large number of returned soldiers have taken advantage of it, and it is in order to allow a still larger number to be insured that I propose this resolution.
As you are aware, Mr. Speaker, a number of soldiers receive pensions, rather ' small in amount, varying from $2.50 to $10, $15 and more a month. The. money derived from these small pensions is not, as a rule, put to the very, best use. The amount is too small to be saved; it is more in the nature of pin money or spending money, so that the soldier derives no real benefit from it. Should the resolution which I propose carry, the soldier will be permitted, on making application to the Board of Pension Commissioners, to have his pension, or such part of it as may be necessary, apply toward the payment of premiums on insurance under the Returned Soldiers' Insurance Act. The premiums are fairly small; the rates are somewhat better than those given by the line companies, and if the soldier is permitted to request that deductions be made from his monthly pension cheque, to be applied upon premiums, he will be in a position to leave his dependents in a much better position should he unfortunately be carried off. I understand that there is no very great objection to the proposal on the part of the Government, except that its adoption might cause some trouble to the Board of Pension Commissioners; they might have to do a little extra work, and there may be some difficulty in connection with changes of pensions. For instance, having passed a new medical examination, a pensioner might be found quite fit, his pension would be cut off-I understand that this is the objection of the Board of Pension Commissioners-the insurance might be dropped. The answer to that is quite plain. In any case the man would be no worse off than he is at present; he would simply have to continue the payments out of his own resources. I do not think I need add anything further by way of explanation. I think the resolution ought to carry.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: PENSION DEDUCTIONS FOR RETURNED SOLDIERS INSURANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this resolution
refers to a matter of some importance, but none the less a matter of administrative detail. It calls for the granting of the privilege to the pensioner of assigning all or part of his pension, thus making it applicable to the support of an insurance policy under the Returned Soldiers' Insurance Act. As hon. members know, particularly those who have been members of the Government, all departments of the Government are opposed to accepting assignments of pay; it is not the practice in any department that any payee from that department shall be permitted to make an assignment to a private citizen, to a company, even to another department, of his or her salary. No doubt, the objection on general grounds is on account of the greater administrative difficulty of being sure of the correct payment. I do not think any matter of mere difficulty or delay should stand in the way of an improvement, particularly if it is to advance or help the position of a returned soldier. I am not sure whether this would help him very much or not. Of course, any soldier now can turn his cheque back just as soon as he receives it.

maintopic: PENSION DEDUCTIONS FOR RETURNED SOLDIERS INSURANCE
speechtext: It will be easier if he never gets it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: PENSION DEDUCTIONS FOR RETURNED SOLDIERS INSURANCE
speechtext:
If he never gets it, he does not bother with it at all; but even if

he does get it, if he gives an assignment of the whole or part of it on his insurance, he can withdraw that assignment at any time he has a mind to. I suppose there would be less possibility-just slightly less -of a withdrawal or a lapse of the insurance if the privilege of assignment were given. I know the Pension Commissioners, doubtless more than any other branch of Government, have difficulty in being certain of the promptness and correctness of their payments. I do not know what the number is, but many cheques are returned every month, not finding their proper destination, and undoubtedly those difficulties would be enhanced if the assignment privileges were given. There is no doubt in the world that errors would creep in.
I think I am justified in saying, at this stage, that I purpose submitting to the House very shortly a resolution calling for the reappointment this session of a joint committee on re-establishment, along the lines of the re-establishment resolution of last session and the session before, though, perhaps, not just in the same wording. That being the case it occurs to me that, this would be a proper subject to submit to that committee. I think, therefore, it would be well, before giving the consent of the House to this resolution, that one or two members or officials of the Pension Board should be heard, so that the House might be advised by the committee who make detailed inquiry, whether it is worth while adopting this plan or not. I, therefore, suggest to the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) that he allow the resolution to be withdrawn, on the understanding that the subject matter of the resolution will be submitted to the joint committee for report this session.

maintopic: PENSION DEDUCTIONS FOR RETURNED SOLDIERS INSURANCE
speechtext:
Only a word in answer
to the Prime Minister. I understand that no other member wishes to speak.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: PENSION DEDUCTIONS FOR RETURNED SOLDIERS INSURANCE
speechtext: I thought, perhaps, the hon. member was about to withdraw his resolution. Of course, if any other hon. member desires to speak, he should do so now.

maintopic: PENSION DEDUCTIONS FOR RETURNED SOLDIERS INSURANCE
speechtext:
With reference to the
remark of the Prime Minister that it has not been the policy of the Government to permit assignments of any moneys due by governments, I will point out to him that, all during the war, assignments of soldiers' pay were not only permitted but, in fact, enforced. Soldiers were forced to assign their pay, for their own good, it was said,

so that, on a matter of principle such as that, the objection would fall to the ground, whereas, in this case the assignment would be simply a voluntary one in what the soldier would consider to be his own interest.
With reference to cheques being returned, it seems to me that the objection of the' Prime Minister would disappear. If the cheques were simply transferred from one department to another, we would have less difficulty in reference to returned cheques; there would be less difficulty with reference to wrong addresses of the pensioners, as the cheques would simply be sent
9 p.m. from the Board of Pension Commissioners direct to the Department of Returned Soldiers' Insurance. The Returned Soldiers' Insurance Act is a new one, and very few of us are familiar with the details of it. The proposition which I make, although I have already made it to the Pension Commissioners, is perhaps new to a large number of the members of this House, so that, in order to give them occasion to study it, I will cheerfully accede to the request of the Prime Minister, on the understanding that the subject matter of the resolution is to receive further consideration during the session. maintopic: PENSIONS TO WIDOWED MOTHERS OF RETURNED SOLDIERS.
PENSIONS TO WIDOWED MOTHERS OF RETURNED SOLDIERS.
speechtext:
moved:
That, in the opinion of this House, it is ex- pedient to amend the Act to provide pensions to or in respect of- members of the Canadian Naval and Military Air Forces, 1919, so as to provide that the pension of a widowed mother of a member of the forces who has died on active service shall not be reduced on account of her Income; and further that pension shall be granted her of right whether or not there are other living children.
He said: Mr. Speaker, as hon. members who have been interested in pensions are doubtless aware, this is by no means a new matter. Since I have been a member of this House, on every occasion on which an opportunity has presented itself, I have brought this subject to the attention of the House of Commons; I have advocated it in committee and on the floor of the House. We have the Pension Act which provides for pensions for disabled ex-soldiers, their dependents, the widows of soldiers, and, to a certain extent, the dependents parents of soldiers. This provision for dependent parents of soldiers is limited in many re-

spects, and, to my mind, it is and has been altogether too limited.
In this resolution I intend to discuss only that phase of the situation which has regard to the widowed mother of a soldier who has been killed overseas. It is my intention that this widowed mother should receive, at the hands of the state, absolutely the same treatment as the actual widow of a soldier killed at the front. There are and have been certain restrictions and limitations to the pensions allotted to the widowed mother. Some of those restrictions I am glad to say, owing to the efforts of those members in the House who have been interested in that class of pensioners, have disappeared. Formerly the widowed mother who earned any money was not allowed to benefit by the Pension Act. We had the sad spectacle of the mother who had given her only son to the cause being obliged, though her age hardly permitted her to work, to engage as scrub woman. This, I am glad to say, has disappeared since the Pension Committee has made the recommendation, which the House has accepted, to the effect that the actual earnings of the widowed mother shall not be taken into account in calculating her pension. But the widowed mother's enjoyment of a pension is limited by statute. By the Pension Act of 1920, it is provided that:
The pension to any parent or person in the place of a parent shall be subject to review from time to time and shall be continued, increased, decreased or discontinued in accordance with the amount deemed necessary by the Commission to provide a maintenance for such parent or person but in no case shall such pension exceed the amount of pension prescribed for parents in schedule B of this Act.
One great complaint we have had hitherto is that the widowed mother, being limited and restricted with reference to her pension, has had to have this pension revised at different times, and the pension itself has always been subject to review. The result has been that in order to keep these pensions straight, a whole horde of inspectors and visitors comes down on the unfortunate woman who receives a pension. We have had cases of these visitors coming in and questioning the poor widow whether or not she was satisfied with the pension she obtained, and by a series of adroit questions finding out that perhaps the poor woman obtained certain sums from insurance on her late husband or that she owned a little piece of property in some other part of the country, or had a few dollars in the bank. All these things were duly reported to headquarters by the
visitor, and headquarters in a large number of cases, I am sorry to say, cut off the pension. There have been numerous complaints as to pensions being cut off in this way; and it is to obviate that difficulty that I am proposing that this pension should not be subject to any review whatsoever, but that once granted it should be granted for good and all. Section 23 of the Pensions Act provides:
When a parent or person in the place of a parent has unmarried sons residing with him or her who should, in the opinion of the Commission, be earning an amount sufficient to permit them to contribute to the support of such parent or person, each such unmarried son shall be deemed to be contributing not less than ten dollars a month towards such support.
You will note that the statute makes reference only to unmarried sons. Now it was well understood, and I think every member of last year's Pensions Committee will bear me out in this, that in no case was the Act to be interpreted in such a fashion as to allow any deductions to be made from a widow's pension on account of the earnings of any married male member of the family or of any female members of the family. If I remember rightly, the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cock-shutt), or the hon. member for East Al-goma (Mr. Nicholson), last year instanced a case where an amount was deducted from a pension because one of the girl members of the family had earned a certain amount of money by working as a stenographer, and at the time the Chairman of the Committee, the hon. member for London (Mr. Cronyn), and the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt), indignantly denied that anything was to be deducted from the widow's pension on account of the earnings of any of the female members of the family. If I have given the wrong names or ascribed to any hon. member things he did not say, I hope he will call my attention to it. Now, how does this work out in practice? I had a case to submit during the course of the summer, one among very many, to the Board of Pension Commissioners. I may state in passing that it is not my intention to attack in any way the Board of Pension Commissioners. I consider they have a very difficult duty to ferform, and that on the whole they have performed it well, but I contend that no such discretion should be given to the Board or to any other Government officials as is given under this Act. It has been the experience, I think, with those who have had to do with Government departments that when we give

too much discretion to Government officials, they are apt to become very officious, and we are apt to find that their discretion is usually not in the best interests of those whose affiairs they are supposed to administer. However, to return to the point I was discussing, of unmarried sons geing presumed to contribute $10 per month, in this particular case I was informed by the Board as follows:
According to your letter W is earning $1,200 per annum. J. is undergoing .treatment for T. B. C. in the S. C. R.
I might say that in this case three sons were at the war; one is now earning a certain amount of money, another owing to war service is now totally disabled and is undergoing treatment in the S. C. R., and it was suggested by the Board of Pension Commissioners that this gentleman undergoing treatment in the S. C. R. for T. B. C. should support on the allowance he gets from the S.C. R. his widowed mother. I will leave that suggestion with those who took part in the deliberations of the Pensions Committee last year. The Board goes on to state:
Further, that the income of the home is $1,500 per annum on account of the earnings of the two daughters.
Because the daughters between them were earning $1,500 this widowed mother was not granted the pension to which she would have been entitled under the Act. Now I submit that under the Act mention is made only of deductions on account of the earnings of an unmarried son residing with the parent, and not in the case of those residing elsewhere, and most certainly not from the earnings of daughters who are obliged owing to the family circumstances to earn their living in the world. Further, paragraph (7) provides, and I think the members of the Pensions' Committee will remember that there was considerable discussion of this point last year:
The pension to a widowed mother shall not be reduced on account of her earnnigs from personal employment or on account of her having free lodgings or so long as she resides in Canada on account of her having an income from other sources which does not exceed two hundred and forty dollars per annum.
The first point is this: If the widowed mother's income exceeds $240 per annum, that is, if she has more than $20 per month, they will have nothing to do with her, they will give her no pension. The widowed mother, in many cases too old to work and utterly incapable of earning her living, is

supposed to be able to get along on a measly $20 per month. I submit that in the judgment of this House we should not force these women, who in many cases have lost their only support, to be obliged to live in such fashion.

speechtext:
The hon. gentleman is wrong
there. I think he must have got a wrong impression from reading the Act. That is not the law at all.

maintopic: PENSIONS TO WIDOWED MOTHERS OF RETURNED SOLDIERS.

maintopic: PENSIONS TO WIDOWED MOTHERS OF RETURNED SOLDIERS.

I am very glad if it is
