speechtext: If the $20 is unearned income, that is, if it < comes from some source other than her own earnings, it is deducted from the maximum she is entitled to, which is $60, and I understand this is the only country in the world where she gets such a maximum.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: PENSIONS TO WIDOWED MOTHERS OF RETURNED SOLDIERS.
speechtext: I have understated it. She may get the $60 in addition to the $20. Up to $20 there is no deduction, but beyond that, if her income is unearned, it may be deducted from the $60. That is the law.

maintopic: PENSIONS TO WIDOWED MOTHERS OF RETURNED SOLDIERS.
speechtext: As a matter of fact that should be the interpretation of the law. But in the correspondence which I have had with the Board of Pension Commissioners that is not the interpretation which has been given it, and that is why I wish to make the matter perfectly clear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: PENSIONS TO WIDOWED MOTHERS OF RETURNED SOLDIERS.
speechtext: Will the hon. member read the letter?

maintopic: PENSIONS TO WIDOWED MOTHERS OF RETURNED SOLDIERS.
speechtext: I have four or five letters, but I should not like to go into the details or to give names.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: PENSIONS TO WIDOWED MOTHERS OF RETURNED SOLDIERS.
speechtext: Very well.

maintopic: PENSIONS TO WIDOWED MOTHERS OF RETURNED SOLDIERS.
speechtext:
I may say, however, that there has been considerable discussion about the matter and I am quite willing to communicate to the Prime Minister the purport of this correspondence. In any case we will suppose that the Prime Minister is right and that the Board of Pension Commissioners do interpret the law in the way they should. I will call the Prime Minister's attention to the fact that section 7 provides that the pension shall not be reduced by reason of earnings so long as the recipient resides in Canada. This would have the effect of precluding all those widowed mothers who reside, let us say, in the United States, in Scotland, or in England. On this point I would remind

63S
the Prime Minister that last year during the discussion of the Pensions Bill certain hon. members, for instance, the hon. member for East Algoma (Mr. Nicholson), the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen s (Mr. Fielding), the hon. member for Guys-borough (Mr. Sinclair) and the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoiia (Mr. McKenzie), pressed this point to such an extent that the then Prime Minister, the right hon. member for King's (Sir Robert Borden), asked that the section be suspended for some time. After this suspension the Prime Minister returned to the House, whilst the discussion of the Bill was still in progress and stated:
I shall certainly take into consideration what has been said on this subject by the hon. gentlemen who have spoken. I see some force in the observation as to the feeling of irritation which might be created by too close or too frequent inquiries into ttie private affairs of persons who have lost near relatives in the war.
This refers to the first point.
But my hon. friends will observe that it will be impossible to change this provision without bringing down another resolution. I hope, therefore, they will be willing to accept my assurance that what they have said in the matter will not be overlooked.
I think that if I had time I could show to the present Prime Minister that the postponement of further consideration of the clause was due, in great part at any rate, to the objections of hon. members on this side as well as across the floor in regard to widowed mothers resident in the United States. Subsection 8 section 23 of the Act says that the pension of a parent or person in place of a parent shall not be reduced on account of the payment of such person of municipal insurance on the life of a deceased member of the forces. I contend that the pension should not be reduced by reason of the payment of any insurance. My contention is that if the deceased young man made his insurance payable to his mother, as in a great many cases good boys do, and paid for it, she should get it and should not have her pension deducted in consequence. As my hon. friend from Brome (Mr. McMaster) reminds me, such payment would not be deducted in the case of a claim for damages. And though this is not a case of a claim for damages against the country, it is a case in which the country has a solemn obligation to fulfil towards these soldiers and their dependents. When the soldiers went to the war it was definitely promised that their people would be no worse off financially, should they be so unfortunate as to lose their lives in the
cause for which the country was fighting, than when they went away, I submit-and this is the whole tenor of my resolution

that the widowed mother should be placed on exactly the same basis as the widow. The widowed mother who lost her son at the front is as a rule well up in years and is unable to earn her living in any way or to increase her income; and it should be the peculiar and special care of the state to look after her. I say that we have possibly a greater obligation towards the widowed mother than towards the widow herself, and it is our duty to see to it that we are not told that the aged mothers of Canadian soldiers are in want or are apt to be in want owing to discriminatory legislation of this Parliament.
I do not think there is very much more' that I need say on this subject. I think, however, that it might perhaps have been better to have discussed it on a day when there was a larger attendance of members. But I see a number of those who in the past have supported the object of this resolution, and I hope that this, the fifth session during which I have brought this matter to the attention of the House, will be the last in which I shall have been obliged to argue in favour of this class of dependents who deserve so much from the country.

maintopic: PENSIONS TO WIDOWED MOTHERS OF RETURNED SOLDIERS.
speechtext:
The
hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Power) will admit that he and I have fought together on this question through several of the pension committees sitting in former years, and sometimes we were practically alone in our fight in that respect. Now I certainly do not want to say anything to-night that would prejudice or pre-judge the position of the widowed mother. No one could have greater sympathy with her than I have. I cannot forget the remark of one of the Chairmen of patriotic funds who, during the course of the war-said he had yet to find a mother who was not broken-hearted because her son went overseas. But throughout not only our pension legislation but that of every other country has run the difference between a pension to a widow and a pension to dependent parents. The widow as the hon. member has said, gets her pension as of right absolutely independently of what her station in life may be; but the parents of the man who has died have always been called upon to prove, first; that they were supported, or might be supported, by the son who had died, and, second; that their financial position was such that they were

really in a dependent position. Once their financial independence was shown their right to a pension ceased. Well, we have improved the position to a certain extent. In the early years of the war the widowed mother only got $22 a month. She gets now, with the bonus awarded during this year, $60 a month. Then she had deducted from her pension her personal earnings. Well, that was corrected. She was, I think, two years ago allowed her personal earnings without any deduction for her pension. Any independent or unearned income which she might receive was deducted from the pension awarded to her; and the Pension Board, as perhaps was their duty, went to some lengths in construing what was an independent income. They held, for instance, that the ownership of a house was equivalent to a certain amout of rental per annum, and while they fixed that rental at a reasonable figure, some $10 or $15 a month, the mother's ownership of that house did result in a reduction in her pension. They also held that if she had sons capable of maintaining her living with her and earning a sufficient income, the duty of maintaining the mother rested on those living sons and that no pension was due. Well, as I say, we corrected some of those things. A widow may now live in her own house and yet we make no reduction from her pension; and as the member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) says, if she is in receipt of an independent income up to $20 a month, no deduction is made on account of that income. That is to say she will get $60 a month by way of pension even if she is in receipt of $20 a month of independent income, or $80 a month altogether. If she gets $25 a month independent income, $5 comes off her pension. If she gets $80 a month independent income she gets no pension at all and, to that extent, she is in an absolutely different position from the widow of a soldier. Then we have also provided under the last Act, as has already been explained, that if the mother had sons living with her who, in the opinion of the Pension Board, were capable of supporting her, those sons should be held to be contributing $10 a month toward the support of their mother. If she only had two such sons, and had no independent income, that would be considered to be equivalent to $20 of unearned income and no deduction would be made from her pension; but if she had more than two sons, or if she had an independent income and two sons living with her, then there might be a deduction of income.

I confess that I am surprised to learn that the Act has been so construed that the earnings of a daughter are deducted or are taken into account. It was certainly not according to my recollection. I have not had the opportunity of looking at the Act recently, but my memory is very clear that so far as the Pension Committee is concerned we only considered and were only considering sons, and the question of daughters or the earnings of daughters never arose.
While one hesitates to mention the ques- . tion of cost in a matter of this kind I think I should point out to the House that the estimate of the cost of the proposed changes which we made last year-those changes which I have tried to outline- represented an increase of nearly two and a half millions in the annual pension bill of the country. It struck me, that that was a very high estimate at the time, but it was the one furnished us by responsible officials and we had to adopt it. I have not yet had any intimation as to how the changes have worked out in actual practise. I believe that we are the only country that has, up to date, made the allowances on behalf of a mother that have been made. As I understand it the greatest amount allowed by any other country to a dependent mother is $48 a month, and all unearned income is deducted from that pension. Perhaps we have not gone far enough yet. I think it is a matter that might very well be again considered if a committee is appointed this session.

maintopic: PENSIONS TO WIDOWED MOTHERS OF RETURNED SOLDIERS.
speechtext:
This is a question which I, with the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power), have fought for a good many years. I am not considering either what the cost to Canada is, or what any other country does; it is a question of whether Canada has done justice to these women or whether she has not. I agree with the hon. member for Quebec South that there has been a great deal of irritation, too much irritation, by having inspectors unnecessarily visit these women. They go around more or less in disguise, they do not know what they are after, and the first thing the recipients know these widows' pensions are cut off, or reduced, and we do not get any reason for such action until we come down here to the Pension Board at Ottawa. I do not think that is fair. Neither do I think it is fair that there should be any discrimination between widows and widowed mothers. While I do not wish to raise the question of discrimination here,

I would certainly say that if any discrimination were to be made it should be made in favour of the mothers. We all know that these women are older as a class than the wives, and their earning power and capacity in life is diminished, compared with the younger set of women who happen to be left widows. In estimating their dependent condition I think the figures have been set altogether too low. For instance you say that a woman is not entitled to a pension unless she is in a dependent condition, and I admit there is a great deal to be said for that.
But then you come down to set a figure, and you set $240 as the limit. That is to say, I think no deduction should be made -and I moved this in committee once or twice last year-where a woman is in receipt of less than $700 or $800 a year. Considering the cost of living to-day, I do think a woman is dependent if she has not that amount of income, and I think a great deal of this trouble might be eliminated if that standard was raised. I realize, of course, that it would not do to put women enjoying an income of $4,000 or $5,000 on a footing of equality with women who have a very small income, but I think it is altogether too low to set the limit at $240.
I agree with the hon. member for Quebec South that we have to make the administration more a matter of routine, and not leave so much to the discretion of the Board of Pension Commissioners. I have nothing but the highest praised for those commissioners. I have found them at all times considerate and more or less generous, but they do have a faculty of interpreting the regulations in a manner which does not always meet with my approval. As I said before, I think we must eliminate all these irritating conditions. I do not think it is fair to deduct from a married woman's pension $10 a month if she has a boy who is not working or whom she is not able to make work. It is pretty bard for a mother to say to her boy, "You have got to work or get out." Sometimes he is not able to work, and sometimes she is absolutely unable to force him, and in a great many cases she has not the heart to do it. In my opinion these pensions should be made a matter of absolute right. I do not think you can put them on any other ground and do justice to the widows and mothers of the soldiers who died in France. I cannot see why any distinction should be made between a boy's mother and a boy's widow when they were both dependent upon him for a living. I also agree
with the hon. member for Quebec South that any insurance they might have coming to them through the generosity of municipalities or firms or societies should not be deducted from their pensions. Surely Canada is big enough and generous enough to pay her own debts to these widows and widowed mothers without taking into consideration such insurance.
I hope that this matter will be settled once for all. I think the Pension Committee in the past has succeeded in eliminating nearly all the defects of the Pension Act. Up to a couple of years ago it had many defects, but during the last year I think the committee has worked admirably, and as far as I have been able to find there are to-day very few complaints indeed. Most of them, I am sorry to say, are associated nearly altogether with the medical men. Consciously or unconsciously, they seem to have got into their system some kind of microbe which impels them to screw pensioners down very often to the lowest possible figure. I do not believe that that is in the best interests of Canada, and I do not believe that such action expresses the will of this House, the will of this Government, or the will of the people.

maintopic: PENSIONS TO WIDOWED MOTHERS OF RETURNED SOLDIERS.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I entirely agree with many of the suggestions thrown out by the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power). My sympathy goes out very largely to the widowed mother. I do not think that we should boast of what Canada has done or is doing for her soldiers. I believe it is the desire of this Government and the wish of the people that none of her soldiers' dependents should suffer one iota. When I was Minister of Militia I suggested in this House that the Government should grant to the mothers who had lost their boys in the war a small silver cross, which I designated The Mother's Cross of Sacrifice. To my mind the greatest sacrifice in this war was made by the mothers who reared their boys and sent them to the battlefront. I know of many instances where a widowed mother has suffered more than any one realizes, and is in fact suffering to-day, and will continue to suffer for the rest of her life. While this country has been generous, and while I for one realize that the Board of Pension Commissioners have done herculean work and that complaints have been few and far between, yet I think the commissioners are forgetting one essential fact in the administration of the Act, namely, that they are dealing with human beings.

maintopic: C36 COMMONS

speechtext: I think there should be a little more human kindness in the administration. I have every confidence in the Prime Minister's assurance that he proposes to move for the appointment of another committee to go into these various matters this session. The committee appointed last year did magnificent work, of which the soldiers and the country heartily approved, as did also this House. If that committee is reappointed I am confident that what has been brought forward by the hon. member for South Quebec, with a portion of which I entirely agree, will have the most careful and sympathetic consideration and that something will be worked out to meet this situation.

maintopic: C36 COMMONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a member of the Pension Committee ever since there was a pension committee of this House, I must confess that I think we considered this question at all our meetings. Somebody has said that the widowed mother is always old. I know a great many widowed mothers that are not any older than the widows of our boys, so that that description is not always appropriate.
As to the limit of $240, the Ontario Government recently passed an Act whereby the widow without children gets $30 a month; the widow with one child, $35 a month; the widow with two children, $40 a month; the mother with three children, $45 a month, and the widow with four children, $50 a month. Our pension to the widowed mother was $60 a month with no deduction for her own earnings, but a deduction for unearned income over $240, leaving $80 a month as explained by the hon. member for London (Mr. Cronyn).
I see no reason why, sons, who are unmarried and living at home, should not assist in supporting their mother or their father, for it encourages thrift on the part of the boys, and, after all, it is their duty. If a mother wants to board her son without charging him anything, why that is her or the family's lookout, but the country should not be called upon to be philanthropic to the extent of making good her indulgence or his default. That sort of philanthropy breeds a type of people who are not of much use in this country. Nobody respects the mother more than I do, whether she be a widow or not a widow, and whether she be in this country or in any other country. But we have gone pretty far in the granting of pensions, and if people are economical and try to get on they will find the pensions ample 
to maintain their families in all decency. Somebody said that the boy who was in a sanitarium was expected to pay something toward the upkeep of his mother, as well as the boy who has been living at home. As I understand it, the boy in the sanitarium is allowed $17 a month for incidental expenses-cigarettes, laundry, and that sort of thing, and the dependent receives $75 a month. No man who is in a sanitarium, no matter where it is located, requires that $75 a month, for he is supplied with everything-nursing, food, and so on.

maintopic: C36 COMMONS
speechtext: Does my hon. friend think that this $75 a month, granted of right to the soldier who has been disabled by war service, should be applied to the unkeep of his dependent mother?

maintopic: C36 COMMONS
speechtext: I do not see why part of it should not be so applied. If the man is disabled he will be pensioned; if he is in the sanitarium only temporarily and subsequently recovers fully, he will not receive a pension when he comes out; he is expected to earn his living in civil life. I have the greatest sympathy for both the widow and the widowed mother, but there is no use in running away with sentiment; it does not assist either the widow or the widowed mother to become independent, to become a good citizen. I repeat that the boy who leaves home and who will not help to support his mother or his father will never become a good citizen. I see no reason why the Government or the Board of Pension Commissioners should make that deduction of $10 a month. It is a very small amount. After all, the pensions throughout are generous. However, this is a question which should be brought before the Pension Committee, if it is going to be appointed, and thrashed out by them; then if the House does not agree with the -report of that Committee, the matter can be further discussed here.

speakeroldname: Mr. T. M. M. TWEEDIE (Calgary West) :
maintopic: C36 COMMONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to support the resolution of the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power). I could never see any justification for a distinction between the pension payable to the widow and wife of the soldier and that payable to the widowed mother. It seems to me that the test is whether the pension is payable as a matter of right or as a matter of dependency, We must adopt either of these two principles as applicable to both class of cases. We have adopted the principle that the widow or wife of the soldier is entitled to

pension as a matter of right, and we endeavour to ascertain what amount will be sufficient to enable her to live comfortably and decently during the time she is in receipt of that pension. We should apply the same principle to the widowed mother and grant her the pension as a matter if right, as in the case of the widow.
The member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) contends that if we pay these sums to widowed mothers as a 'matter of right, there will be a tendency to breed in this country a class of people entirely dependent upon the Government for support. But if he stands by that argument he must also apply it to the widow or wife of the soldier who was killed at the front, because many a man who was killed at the front left behind him sons who are just as -capable of supporting his widow-their mother-as the brothers of a man killed overseas are capable of supporting their widowed mother. I think it is simply a matter of right that the widowed mother should be classed with the widow of the soldier, and that pensions should be paid to her without any deductions on account of insurance or other income from independent sources. When the Committee are considering this question they can bear in mind the opinions which have been expressed in the House tonight in connection with the matter, and if they do I should think that they they would bring in a report along the lines I have suggested. Should they fail to do so the House will be at liberty to deal with the matter on a subsequent occasion. I have much pleasure in supporting the arguments which have been submitted to the House by the hon. member for Quebec South.	'

maintopic: C36 COMMONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have much pleasure in supporting the views of the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power). This is a question which has been before the. Pension Committee for some time. I believe that in every case the widowed mother should be treated in just the same way as the dependent widow. There is another question in connection .with this matter which has come to my mind during the progress of the debate, and that is the position of the woman who marries the returned soldier who dies subsequent to his injury from any cause. As the member for Muskoka rightly said, our medical men are apt to interpret the law very closely, and in many cases the widow of a returned soldier is left without any assistance from
the Government simply because she married a soldier after his return to Canada. We find that men who returned to Canada 90 or 75 or 60 per cent, disabled receive for themselves, their wives and children, an amount of pension proportionate to their disability, while the wife of the soldier, whom she married after his return to Canada and who subsequently died, receives nothing. These aspects of the question should be taken into consideration by the Committee and reported upon favourably.

maintopic: C36 COMMONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not like to let this opportunity pass without again expressing my sympathy with the object of the resolution moved by the member for Quebec South (Mr. Power). I have, on two or three previous occasions, spoken very strongly in favour of the utmost liberality as regards the treatment of the widowed mother of a soldier. While her pension has been improved in many respects, I feel it is hardly yet as liberal as I should like to see it. I admire the spirit that actuates the hon. member for Oxford North (Mr. Nesbitt) in keeping down the expenses of the country as far as possible-and, perhaps, there are too few of us who take that course-but I feel that in the present case the committee have not yet been over liberal. I know of a few cases in which hardship has resulted. I have always taken the ground-and I do not see any reason for changing it-that when men have died, as these men have, in the interest of this country and the Empire, we owe them a different debt from that which we may owe to any other class of citizens. The hon. member for Oxford North has related what has been done in Ontario with regard to pensions for widows, but it ought to be remembered that the widows who are provided for by the Ontario Act have become widows by an act of Providence.

maintopic: C36 COMMONS
speechtext: What about the others? Was that not an act of Providence?

maintopic: C36 COMMONS
speechtext:
Just a moment.
The one has become a widow by an act of Providence, and in the other case the soldier has died in the service of his country. I consider that there is a greater responsibility upon the country when a man dies in its service than there is in the case of a man who has died without giving any particular service to his country. I hope, of course, all citizens do some service to their country, and J do not say they do not; but this country owes a certain debt to the

man who has died at the front or on account of illness that he has contracted at the front, by reason of the sacrifice that has been made, and if we cannot pay that debt to the man, we can pay it to the widow. There is quite a strong difference, and deductions should not be made by reason of the earnings of the widowed mother.

maintopic: C36 COMMONS
speechtext: They are not.

maintopic: C36 COMMONS
speechtext:
Yes, they are. I remember a case that I have brought up two or three times before the Pension Board and it is not yet settled. Because the widow has up to the present been able to earn a fairly good living, she is denied a pension. The late member for York-Sunbury (Mr. McLeod) also brought up the same matter and, so far as I know, it has never been settled because the widow is able to earn a certain amount in a banking institution, and' if the amount is above the specific amount that has been named, nothing is done. They tell her that if she finally becomes incapacitated so that she cannot work, her case will be taken into consideration, but not as long as she can earn what is possibly a fairly good living for a widow. She is, however, working beyond her years, and the day will soon be at hand when she cannot continue to work. The country owes a debt to that widow
10 p.m. whether she is willing and able to go out and earn her daily bread or not; she may wish to lay up something for a rainy day, and the country should not be so severe in making deductions from the pension of a widow simply because she is able to earn a certain amount for her sustenance. I speak very strongly in this connection. I know the hon. member for Oxford North does not agree with me-and I am sorry for that because I esteem his judgment as very valuable-but at the same time I believe, if he opens up his heart-strings a little more, the country will not find fault with him in that respect. I believe in being absolutely generous to the widows and widowed mothers of returned soldiers. If we do anything to lighten the burden and to make them forget some of the sad loss that they have sustained as a result of this war, we are doing what is simply our duty and the most liberal treatment we can give is not too much in connection with the resolution that my hon. friend (Mr. Power) has put on the Order Paper. I am pleased to add a word on behalf of this matter and I trust, if a committee is

appointed, this matter will be further con sidered and I am sure it will meet the views of a large number of the members of this House if even more generous treatment is given to the widows and widowed mothers of returned soldiers.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Shelburne and Queen's) :
maintopic: C36 COMMONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) is to be congratulated on having presented this matter to the House in such a form as to win, as it has, a large measure of sympathy from hon. members. I have such a high appreciation of the work done by the committee that sat during the last two years under the able chairmanship of the hon. member for London (Mr. Cronyn), that I would be reluctant to see any change made in the matter of pensions without having the matter first submitted to the committee. I hope from the expressions of opinion given by hon. members this evening that the committee will be able to concur in the case presented by the hon. member, but, at all events, an opportunity will be given for considering it. I know the object of these deductions, and it is a good one. The idea is that you do not want to pay pensions to people who do not need them. That is a very commendable object; but if we have regard to the number of pensions generally, are there enough cases of that kind to make it worth while to make that regulation? In making these deductions with the resultant worry and interference, is the game worth the candle? The number of wealthy people in Canada is not very great; in this country wealth is fairly equally and comfortably distributed-and that is better than a few people having the wealth as is the case in some countries-so that if you had no deductions at all, the number of widows who would get a pension and who did not need it, would not be very large, and if they got a little more, no great harm would be done. The suggestion of the hon. member for Muskoka (Mr. P. McGibbon) is that, unless it can be shown that the widow is in receipt of a very substantial sum from other quarters, the wise policy would be to have no deductions at all. I would suggest to the hon. member for Quebec South that, having made the progress he has in the good work, he consent to let the matter go to the committee and bring it up at a later date, if that be necessary.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) :
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: C36 COMMONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it affords me a

great deal of pleasure to join with the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) in congratulating the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Powers) upon the manner in which he has brought his motion forward, and upon the reception with which his presentation of it has been met. There is no doubt that the case of the widowed mother is one that appeals most strongly to the sympathies of all of us. I am sure that we would all desire that every means should be taken to prevent its happening that any mother who has lost her son in the service of this country should be left in any condition approaching even to want. Of course, when you come to carry out your desires, there are some considerations that have to be borne in mind, because, after all, you have to arrive at some definite sum. Some consideration ought to be given to equality. While you may avoid laying down an absolute rule as to what particular amount of income, independent of other sources than the pension, should lead to deductions being made from a pension, still, it does rather appeal to one that a good deal is to be said against granting pensions to people with regard to whom it is absolutely impossible to suggest that there can be any need. It has occurred to me, listening to the discussion, that one way of meeting the situation, and perhaps a fairer way-I am not expressing any conclusion; this is only what occurred to me-might lie in the direction of increasing the maximum amount of sixty dollars that is to be given as a pension, rather than in directing one's attention solely to the question of what deductions, if any, ought to he made.
However, I do not desire to express any final opinion on the subject this evening. I think the hon. member for South Quebec (Mr. Power) can rest assured that the matter will engage the serious, and I do not think I would be going too far in saying, the sympathetic attention of the committee. I would join with my hon. friend from Shel-burn and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) in asking the hon. member for South Quebec, if with the assurance that the matter will he brought to the attention of the committee, and seriously, and carefully, and I think I may say, sympathetically looked into by them, he might not think it proper at the present time to withdraw his motion.
Mr. THOMAS W. CALDWELL (Victoria and Carleton, N.B.) :	As a member
of last year's Pension Committee it would probably not be amiss for me to say a
word in this discussion. I supported the hon. member for South Quebec (Mr. Power) when he moved this resolution before the Pension Committee last year. When the resolution was defeated in the committee it was only by a very small majority, and I felt at the time, and still feel, that if the whole committee had been present when the vote was taken it would have carried.
There is one other case I wish to bring to the notice of the House and of the committee, and it is that of the widow of the soldier who was wounded or disabled overseas and who marries after his return to Canada. His widow is absolutely denied a pension under the present Act. I would like to see this injustice to the large number of widows of returned soldiers who have married subsequent to their disability remedied this session. I also agree with the hon. member for Muskoka (Mr. McGibbon) that the sum of $240 per annum is too small an amount of income to allow before deductions are made from the pension. I fully agree with my hon. friend from Muskoka that no deduction should be made from the widow's pension on an unearned income of less than $700 or $800 a year. In view of the fact that a pension committee is to be appointed this year, I think it would be the part of wisdom for my hon. friend from South Quebec to let this matter go before that committee, and I think there is very little question that these matters will be remedied in accordance with his resolution.
Mr. DANIEL D. McKENZIE (Cape Breton North and Victoria) : There is just one phase of this subject that I should like to bring to the notice of the House, and particularly of the hon. member for London (Mr. Cronyn), who was chairman of the Pension Committee last, year and who in the natural course of events will be chairman this year if another committee is appointed. I appreciate very much the forceful and very proper way in which the hon. member for South Quebec (Mr. Power) has placed the subject before the House, and I am sure the discussion that has taken place, and the experiences that several members have given, will be of assistance to the committee when they come to consider these questions.
There is one point I would like to impress upon the House, and that is in connection with the deductions that are made from the pension in cases where there happen to be two or more sons. I know that in the part of the country from which I come there are many cases where there are perhaps

one or two sons who should support their mother, but who will not, and what is the good of throwing the impossible burden on the widow of compelling these boys to support her? There are lots of boys who will not do so, and unless they are supporting their mother voluntarily and freely, it is not right to say that the mothef shall suffer because they are not doing their duty. In cases of that kind, where the widowed mother cannot increase her income except by what her boys might give, I would certainly say to the House and to the committee, whoever they may be, that they might very well leave out of consideration making any deduction from the pension of the widow.

maintopic: C36 COMMONS
speechtext: May I ask whether these boys live at home with the mother?

maintopic: C36 COMMONS
speechtext:
In some cases they
do and perhaps in a niggardly way pay their board. My hon. friend from South Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) knows that boys sometimes take advantage of their mother when they are boarding and rooming with her that they would not take of other people, and will not pay as much for their board as they would have to pay elsewhere. I know cases of that kind, where the mother has to do the washing, for instance, and give the board cheaper - than the boys could get it elsewhere. The boys will pay just the amount they were paying before prices went up, and the mother is the loser. That is all the profit she gets from boarding her boys. I do not wish to give a bad name to the people in my part of the country, but there are cases of that kind, and I think I am more than justified in bringing them to the attention of the committee. I repeat that the committee should leave out their consideration making deductions from the pension of a widow who has sons who might support her, but who are not doing so.
I wish particularly to bring to the notice of the House the case of some widows who are not receiving a pension at all, and so far as I know, have not received any consideration from the Government so far. It is within the knowledge of the Minister of Militia and Defence (Mr. Guthrie), the exminister (Mr. Mewburn), and other members of this House that at certain stages of the war, in 1915, 1916, and perhaps later, this Government engaged some steamers to carry supplies to the old country, iron and steel, for instance, from Sydney, for the purposes of the war on the other side of the water. These steamers were engaged

for that war service, and I have one particularly in mind at the present moment, the ".Sharon," owned, I think, in Quebec. She was chartered by the Department of Railways and Canals, loaded with steel at Sydney, and started for the other side of the water, but she never got across. The belief is that she was torpedoed. At all events, she never reached the other side, and all on board were lost. Sixteen or seventeen, perhaps twenty, widows were left in my toVn by reason of the loss of the " Sharon." Now if the steamer was torpedoed, and there being no evidence to the contrary it is not a great stretch of the imagination to believe she was, while engaged by the Government of this country for the purposes of the war, these men lost their lives by reason of the war, and it does not take very close reasoning to show that their widows are entitled to some consideration at the hands of the people of this country, and of this Parliament. I would like to have cases of this kind kept in mind by the committee when they come to consider the other features that have been brought to their notice. These steamers that were chartered were not war vessels, but they were used for the purpose of carrying supplies to be used for war purposes, and while the " Sharon" was so engaged these men lost their lives by reason of the unsafe condition of navigation. I would urge that as just as good a case for consideration by the committee as if the men had been killed at the front.

maintopic: C36 COMMONS
speechtext:
It has been alleged during the course of this discussion, or at least it has been suggested, that in some cases the widowed mother obtained more than the widow herself and that she should be very well off with the sum of, say, $80 per month. Now, I am not asking for $80, I simply ask that she be given $60 per month in exactly the same way as the widow obtains it, and without there being any deduction whatsoever. I ask that she be given it of right, that there be no question as to whether she has a house, as to whether she lives in the house which she owns, whether she is keeping a boardinghouse or has turned it into an apartment house, deriving an income therefrom, whether she has a few dollars in the bank, or whether a few dollars were left to her from insurance, or any other consideration of that kind. The point I wish to make quite clear to the House is that to my mind, the widowed mother of the soldier is entitled to be placed by this country in exactly the same position as the widow

of the soldier. I have been told also that we should encourage the widowed mother to become independent. It seems to me that the mother of a boy who has been killed at the front has usually reached an age when it is no business of the country to try to encourage her to become independent; it is rather its duty to see that she is independent. We are not going to set up a school to teach the elderly women who have sacrificed their all in the great war how to become independent in this country. There is no question to my mind of the opinion of the House on this matter, I think that every hon. member will agree with me that this is no time to bring this question before the House. What the province of Ontario does with regard to mothers' pensions is one matter. I do not care what it does. But what the Dominion of Canada does with regard to the, mothers of the sons whom she sent to the front is a matter with which we are all concerned. We have our pledged word to these boys; we have our pledged word in the face of the whole Dominion of Canada; and it seems to me that the least a House of Commons such as this, elected during the war and in the war spirit, can do is to keep its war pledges.
Now, I have been asked to allow this matter to be referred to committee. As I said before, for four years I have been fighting the case of the widowed mothers, and have spoken in furtherance of it in committee; and on each occasion, I am sorry to say, the committee refused to bring in- a favourable report. Last year, I submitted this identical resolution, which a number of hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House and to my left supported. It was referred to the Pension Committee, amidst, I may say, the acclamation of the entire House of Commons. But when the Pension Committee reported they were too busy reporting on other things to have anything to say in favour of the widowed mother, except for a very small amendment to the law as it stood. And when, not being satisfied with the decision of the Pension Committee, either last year or the year before, I carried the matter to the floor of the House, where it was discussed, I was told first that if this point were to be insisted upon, The whole matter would have to be referred back to the committee and in that event it would be held up because the committee would not have time to report before the end of the session. This has been the case for two or three years in succession.
Whenever the report of the Pension Committee came in, we who wished to critise or amend it or to refer it back to the committee were told: Well, we are very willing to help you, and you are possibly right in what you say, but if you oppose this committee's report, no report at all will be brought in and the pensioners will not have the benefit of these provisions. Last session, in spite of this objection made by the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden), I insisted on pushing the matter and I desired to bring it to the vote. On asking the Chair to put the question to the vote, however, I was ruled out of order because, had the law been amended in the direction I proposed, it would have been necessary first to obtain a resolution of the House, as there was involved the question of voting larger sums from the exchequer. This has happened in two years. Now, I have no guarantee that it will not happen again. There is no guarantee that the Pension Committee's report will not be brought down in the dying days of the session and that the Government will not say again: Unless you accept this report and swallow it holus-bolus the pensioners will be deprived of the benefit thereof. And there is equally na guarantee that if I insist on bringing this amendment before the House it will not again be ruled out of order. As a matter of fact, it should be ruled out of order if the chairman of the committee did his duty properly, so that I should be absolutely without recourse. We have a proposition which has -been received by the House with enthusiasm for two, three and, four years, and every time we came to what I might call a show-down the matter was thrown out.

maintopic: C36 COMMONS
speechtext:
Did the hon. member
ever bring that proposition to a vote in this House?

maintopic: C36 COMMONS
speechtext: In order to explain more fully to the hon. gentleman, who has evidently not understood what I have been talking about for the last five minutes, I will tell him that last year I endeavored to bring the matter to a vote but that it was thrown out by the chairman on the ground that I was not in order in proposing that further moneys be voted from the Crown at the request of a private member without a resolution of the House.

maintopic: C36 COMMONS
speechtext:
The hon. member was
a member of the committee whose actions he is complaining of, but he did not bring in a minority report.

maintopic: C36 COMMONS
speechtext: I will answer that question too. For the last three years, on every occasion when the committee brought in a report, I have objected to the omission of any provision for the widowed mother. On every occasion when the matter has been brought before this House I have insisted on these provisions such as I have advocated to-night being placed in the bill. And if the hon. gentleman had the interest of the pensioners and their dependents so much at heart, as I am sure he should have- and as I am sure he would have but for the fact that probably he is under-

maintopic: C36 COMMONS
speechtext: You are not answering the question.

maintopic: C36 COMMONS
speechtext: What is your question?

maintopic: C36 COMMONS
speechtext:
Have you brought in
any minority report?

maintopic: C36 COMMONS
speechtext:
I did on one occasion
bring in a minority report, but I was all alone on this question, and not having had any satisfaction in introducing such a report, I proposed, with the consent and, I think, with the knowledge of all members of the committee to debate this matter on the floor of the House. And as a matter of fact I did debate it on the floor of the House. It is no new question and the hon. gentleman ought to know that. Speaking frankly, I am somewhat reluctant to agree to the request made by the Minister of Justice and my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding). Another reason is that personally I am under the impression that the returned soldiers have no longer very much faith in this Pension Committee. I rather think that in the past few years they have been looking at the Pension Committee and the Committee on Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment as a means of thwarting what they consider to be their, legitimate desires. Last year we had somewhat of a tempest in a teapot but we saw at that time what the true feelings of the soldiers were with reference to the Pension Committee. I am willing to do my best for the returned soldiers at any time, but I will certainly not sit on the committee another year. I know that on several occasions during the proceedings of the committee last year, the soldier vote was defeated by an almost entirely civilian vote; and if that is to happen again-and it might very well happen on this very question-I do not see any necessity or any reason why the committee should sit another year. I have on every possible occasion placed my views

on this important matter before the committee and before the House, and I do not think I could serve any useful purpose by sitting on the committee another year. Nevertheless, I have to bear in mind that if this question were not referred to a committee at the present time my proposition might be defeated, and in all likelihood would result in a worse condition for the poor people whom I am endeavouring to benefit. I am strongly desirous of furthering the cause of the widowed mothers, and if it were left to my own feelings in the matter I would say, "Let us come to a show-down and see whether those who have been telling us so much about their interest in the returned soldiers and their dependents will prove their interest by their votes on the question when put to them in a fair and straightforward manner." However it seems to be the opinion of those who are better versed in parliamentary matters than I am, that more good may perhaps be obtained by referring this question again to a committee; that there may be a better chance of the committee this year seeing things in their true light than has been the case in the past three or four years. Therefore, at the request of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's, for whose opinion I maintain the highest respect, I beg leave to withdraw the motion.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: C36 COMMONS
speechtext:
Is it the pleasure of the House that the hon. gentleman have leave to withdraw the motion?
Motion withdrawn.
On motion of Right Hon. Mr. Doherty the House adjourned at 10.32 p.m.
Tuesday, March 8, 1921.
